draft.title: Scientific notation for small numbers
card: Scientific notation writes a number as a × 10ⁿ, where a is from 1 to less than 10. A very small number, between 0 and 1, uses a negative power of 10.
To write a small number, move the decimal point right until you have a number from 1 to less than 10. The power of 10 is minus the number of places you moved it.
Example: 0.000 52. Move the point 4 places right to get 5.2. So 0.000 52 = 5.2 × 10⁻⁴.
To go back, move the point left by the number in the power. 3 × 10⁻² = 0.03, because the point moves 2 places left. A negative power makes a small number, not a negative number.
draft.remember: A small number is a × 10⁻ⁿ, where n counts the places the point moved to get a.

a.q: A cell is 0.000 073 m wide. How is this written in scientific notation?
a.why: The point moves 5 places right to give 7.3, so the power is −5. Using −4 is tempting, but it comes from counting only the zeros after the point, which is 4, and missing a place.
a.clue: Count the places the point moves to get 7.3.

b.q: A dust particle has a width of 2.5 × 10⁻³ m. What is this as an ordinary decimal?
b.why: A power of −3 means the point moves 3 places left: 2.5 becomes 0.0025. The option 0.025 moves it only 2 places. A negative power does not make the number negative.
b.clue: Move the point 3 places to the left.
